Captivate

/KAP-tih-vayt/ - the stress falls on KAP · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Captivate means to get the attention of, hold.

The eclipse captivated the whole schoolyard for the full four minutes of totality — not one phone came out.

Worked Example

An audiobook narrator with a gravelly voice captivated the carful of cousins so completely that they sat in the driveway, engine off, through the final chapter.

Captivate is stronger than interest or entertain: it means attention is held — taken captive — so that looking away stops being an option. The word remembers its root: a captivated audience is a captured one, if only until the lights come up.

How Captivate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

fascinate

fascinate: to hold interest strongly, especially the mind's

enchant

enchant: to delight as if by magic — warmer, more charmed than held

Antonyms

bore

bore: to lose the room entirely

repel

repel: to drive attention away in distaste

How Strong Is It? — interest → captivate → mesmerize

interest vs. captivate

interest vs. captivate: To interest someone is merely to make them lean in; captivate is stronger — once captivated, they cannot easily lean back out.

mesmerize vs. captivate

mesmerize vs. captivate: Mesmerize goes further than interest ever could, and a step past captivate too: a captivated listener could still look away; a mesmerized one has lost the choice.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — capt

Root — capt: seized, taken (Latin capere, captus)

Suffix — -iv-

Suffix — -iv-: adjective-forming (as in captive)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Capt- (seized) + -iv- + -ate = to take captive. English uses this root for every kind of seizing: capture takes a thing, a captor takes a person, and captivate takes your attention — the gentlest capture in the family, and the only one its prisoner enjoys.

Use the root in a new word: capture

Use the root in a new word: capture: Rangers worked all morning to capture the young bear that had wandered into the campground.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Use captivate when attention is genuinely held, not just caught — a face in a crowd catches your eye; a storyteller captivates the room. It is transitive: something captivates someone. Fascinate stresses the mind's grip and enchant adds delight; captivate sits between them — and its unit-mate winsome names the kind of charm that often does the captivating.
